content.comment_body: Hello everyone. I'm facing the same issue. I set the IP of my [product_name] to 192.168.1.38 and opened port 8080 for it. My public IP is something like xx.xx.xx.xx. When I try to connect using xx.xx.xx.xx:8080 from the internet, I can't establish a connection. Not sure what I'm missing. Hope to get some feedback soon.
Can you clarify what you're trying to achieve? Do you want to access the webserver over the Internet?

Yes, that's correct. Currently, I can only connect when I'm on my local network. How can I access my server from outside my network? I assumed entering my public IP with port 8080 would be enough. Appreciate your response.
You'll need to set up port forwarding for this to work, but be aware it exposes your home network to risks. Using DynDNS or a VPN is a safer alternative.

I believe I've already set up port forwarding. I opened port 700 and linked it to my [product_name] IP (192.168.1.44). When I test within my local subnet using 192.168.1.44:700, it doesn't work, but 192.168.1.44:8080 does. It seems the device continues to use port 8080 despite the forwarded port. Is 8080 the default port? I thought most devices defaulted to port 80. Thanks for your input.

Port forwarding involves more than just opening a port. It requires a specific function on the router, which may or may not be supported. Traffic on port 700 of your router could be directed to port 8080 of the [product_name]. I’ve attached instructions for configuring this on a Fritz!Box router. For example, forwarding port 8030 on the router to 8080 on the [product_name].
Alright, I'll give it a try later. Was the IP in your screenshot the IP address of your [product_name]? Thanks for your assistance.
Yes, the IP shown belongs to one of the [product_name] devices.

Hi [user_name], I tried port forwarding but it still doesn't work. I've included two screenshots in the zip file: one showing my forwarding setup and how port 8080 works in my subnet; the other showing my phone, which isn’t successful using the public IP and port 8030. The issue seems unusual. Regards.
For troubleshooting, ignore the [product_name] temporarily. Set up port forwarding for your PC’s IP, run Wireshark, and attempt an external connection.

DynDNS and VPN serve different purposes. DynDNS helps you use a fixed domain instead of a variable IP address. VPNs, SSH tunneling, and similar solutions enable secure access from outside your network. This applies to any internal device, not just the [product_name], when remote access is required.
I didn’t state they were identical. Still, DynDNS is safer than simple port forwarding.
Hello, thank you for the response. I'll test your suggestion, but first I want to be sure if I’m missing a step. It appears my setup matches what [user_name] did—where might the error lie? Regards.
Seems like it’s a language misunderstanding. Networking real-world examples are helpful: for instance, pretzel isn't better than beer, but makes a great pairing.

Your ISP could be blocking certain ports. First, verify your router’s WAN port has a public IP. Evidence of this would help. For further testing, exclude the [product_name], use a PC with Wireshark, visit an online port scanning tool, start a scan, and check the network activity locally.

analysis.insight_summary: Users are struggling to remotely access a [product_name] webserver through port forwarding, with confusion over default ports and configuration steps. There is a lack of clarity about the effectiveness and safety of port forwarding versus other solutions like DynDNS and VPN. Advice often highlights network security and suggests diagnostic tools, revealing some frustration and knowledge gaps regarding networking basics.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect to set up remote access to their [product_name] webserver by configuring port forwarding and referencing their public IP and port number, assuming this will enable external connectivity just as easily as on their local network. They anticipate that modifying the forwarded port will grant outside access with minimal setup.
